lessons.title: Serial rules, parallel hardware
lessons.summary: A 4-bit counter. The hardware computes both next values at once; XBlue lets you read, and prove, the cycle one rule at a time.
text: The hardware is parallel. In each clock cycle the counter computes both candidate next values at once, count + 1 and 0, and a multiplexer at the end picks one. Open the SystemVerilog tab: _t4 = _t3 ? (count + 1) : count is tick, and _t6 = _t5 ? 0 : _t4 is clear. Both data paths sit side by side.

XBlue reads it in order. schedule tick ≫ clear says: run tick, then run clear, which sees what tick wrote. A rule is atomic: its guard decides whether all of its writes happen. So the next count is two small steps, one after the other, instead of a priority between parallel paths.

The proof follows the story. Below the module, spec writes the cycle as those two steps, and next_eq_spec proves that the design itself (mkCounter.design.cycle) computes exactly spec, for every input and every count. Lean checks all 64 cases with decide. Facts such as reset_wins then follow from the story in one line each.
The hardware agrees. The lowering to VBlue is proved correct (lower_correct), so these theorems hold for the SystemVerilog too.
interfaces is an implicit rule that drives every method output; it runs first.
try: Swap the schedule to clear ≫ tick. Lean now reports that next_eq_spec is false. Rewrite spec in the new order, and restate reset_wins: what does a reset do now?
Prove that the counter never wraps: when it is full and there is no reset, it stays at 15.

lessons.title: A FIFO with guarded enq / deq
lessons.summary: Two rules in parallel (∥) on a 4-entry queue; the guards encode full and empty.
text: enq fires only when there is room, deq only when there is data: the guard is the handshake. Both can fire in one cycle.
a ∥ b runs both sides on the same start-of-cycle state. That is only meaningful when they write different state, and the front end checks it: two sides of ∥ may not write the same register.
That is why count has its own rule: occupancy fires when exactly one of enq / deq does. data[wp] <= … writes one element of a vector register.
try: Move count <= count + 1; into enq (and delete occupancy). Compile: the front end rejects the ∥.
Change the schedule to (enq ≫ deq ≫ occupancy) ≫ clear. Does the trace change? (It should not: the rules write disjoint state.)

lessons.title: A round-robin arbiter
lessons.summary: Combinational logic as named values: rotate, priority-select, rotate back.
text: Most of this design is values (Bit#(8) twice = {req, req};): they are expressions over the current state, recomputed wherever they are used. Only last is state.
priority case takes the first arm whose condition holds; unique case would OR the arms (one-hot). Shifts may take a narrower amount, which is zero-extended.
The grant is a method, so it is computed by interfaces from this cycle's last; advance records the winner for the next cycle.
try: Set req to 0xf (all request): the winner should rotate 0, 1, 2, 3, 0, …
Make it a fixed-priority arbiter by replacing start with 0. Compare the gate count and depth with round robin.

lessons.title: GCD: rules as an algorithm
lessons.summary: Euclid by subtraction; the guards say when each step applies.
text: Each rule is one step of the algorithm, guarded by when the step is legal: swap when x < y, subtract when x ≥ y. Exactly one applies while y ≠ 0.
Because the schedule chains them with ≫, subtract sees the result of a swap in the same cycle: a swap costs no extra cycle. That chaining is real hardware: look at the longest path in Gates.
The stimulus loads gcd(48, 18) at cycle 1 and gcd(105, 30) at cycle 20; watch io_done and io_result.
try: Move subtract before swap in the schedule. Count the cycles until io_done for gcd(48, 18).
Try swap ∥ subtract: both write x, so it is rejected.

lessons.title: A pipelined multiplier
lessons.summary: Two stages; ordering the stage rules latest-first gives pipeline registers.
text: In XBlue a register written by one rule is visible to the rules after it in the same cycle. Put the later pipeline stage first (stage2 ≫ stage1) and every stage reads its predecessor's old value: each register is a pipeline boundary.
Stage 1 multiplies by each nibble of b; stage 2 adds the shifted partial products. out_p is in_a × in_b from two cycles earlier.
Gates shows the cost: two 16×16 multipliers before optimisation, narrowed by wreduce.
try: Swap to stage1 ≫ stage2: stage 2 now sees stage 1's new values and the latency drops to one cycle. Check the longest path.
Compute the whole product in one rule (p <= a16 * zeroExtend(in_b);) and compare depth.

lessons.title: Cache-line state machine
lessons.summary: Valid / dirty bits for four lines, one operation per request.
text: valid and dirty are Vector#(4, Bool) registers; valid[req_line] <= True writes one element chosen at run time.
Each line moves Invalid → Clean (read miss) → Dirty (write) → Invalid (evict, with a writeback if dirty). The guards select exactly one of the op rules per request.

countWb runs after evict in the chain, so it reads valid and dirty after evict cleared them. Its guard held at the start of the cycle but not where it runs: the Simulation pane marks it blocked (amber). Is writebacks ever incremented?
try: Fix the writeback counter: move countWb before evict in the schedule, or fold the increment into evict.
Add a flush op (req_op == 3) that clears every dirty bit.

lessons.title: Schedules decide throughput
lessons.summary: A 2-stage pipeline whose rate depends only on the order of ≫.
text: Each stage rule is guarded by its slot being free. With drain ≫ exec ≫ fetch, each rule sees the slot its successor freed this cycle, so all three fire every cycle and the pipeline moves one item per cycle.
Reverse it and each stage sees its successor still full: the guard is false, a bubble. The Simulation pane's rule strip shows the gaps.
With out_ready low for four cycles the pipeline fills and stalls; the guards alone stop each stage, no extra control logic.
try: Change the schedule to fetch ≫ exec ≫ drain ≫ clear and compare how often fetch fires.
Try (exec ∥ fetch): both write v1, so the front end rejects it.

lessons.title: Exercise: fix the credit counter
lessons.summary: Two bugs: one the compiler finds, one the simulation finds.
text: A sender has 4 credits. take spends one per request, give returns one per response; io_ok checks credits + inflight == 4.
First, it does not compile. The error is on the schedule line: what do take and give both write?
Once it compiles, simulate. io_ok drops at some cycle: step there, look at credits, and find the guard that lets it happen.
try: Hint 1: take ≫ give lets both fire in one cycle, and give sees take's new credits.
Hint 2: with 4 in flight, credits is 0. Should take fire?

lessons.title: A router's matrix arbiter
lessons.summary: From the CcNoc router: a priority matrix that gives the last winner the lowest priority.
text: Each output port of the CcNoc router (XBlue/Examples/CcNoc/Router.lean) has an arbiter like this one, cut here to 3 requesters. Bit 3*i+j of pb says requester i is above j; a requester wins when no requester above it asks.

permit and winner are functions over an Integer index: the front end unrolls them at elaboration, so the hardware is plain gates. pb[k : k] <= v writes one bit; the writes of one rule are put back together into one register write.
The update moves the winner to the bottom: its row is cleared and its column set. That is the whole fairness argument: a requester that keeps asking loses to everyone who was waiting.
try: Hold all three requests high (req = 7) and watch io_grant rotate 1, 2, 4.
Swap the schedule to clear ≫ update: at a reset cycle with requests, the matrix is now left half-updated.

lessons.title: A blocking cache
lessons.summary: The shape of the CcNoc L2 slice: hits from the arrays, a miss walks a small state machine.
text: The CcNoc system's caches (stage 1, ported from Bluespec) are blocking: while a miss is being served, req_ready is low and nothing else gets in. This one has 4 lines of 8 bits.

RegFiles are arrays: a read sees the start of the cycle, and an upd lands at the clock edge. That is the semantics of a Bluespec register too, which is why the port keeps the caches' metadata in arrays.

The miss states are rules with exclusive guards on state, and the order matters: a rule sees what earlier rules of the cycle wrote. The schedule runs them backwards, fill ≫ writeBack ≫ access, so each state lasts one cycle. (In the Bluespec original every rule reads state at the start of the cycle; the port keeps that by testing a start-of-cycle copy.)
try: Keep mem_rvalid low for longer (0*8 1): the cache stays in Fill and refuses requests.
Reverse the schedule to access ≫ writeBack ≫ fill ≫ clear: a miss now runs through WriteBack in the same cycle it is taken.

lessons.title: MSHRs: misses that do not block
lessons.summary: Two miss registers: hit-under-miss, miss-under-miss, and secondary misses merged.
text: Stage 2 of the CcNoc tutorial replaces the blocking L1 with a non-blocking one (L1NB.lean). Its heart is a small file of MSHRs: a miss takes a free one and asks memory; a load to a line that already has an MSHR waits on it (a secondary miss, merged: no second request); a hit is answered at once, even with misses outstanding.
Reg#(Vector#(2, Mshr)) mshr is one register holding two structs; mshr[i] <= … writes one element and e with { f = v } updates one field.
fill ≫ load: a fill frees its MSHR before the load rule runs, so the same cycle can reuse it. Count the requests on mem_req against the loads: the difference is secondary_misses.
try: Give all loads the same line (ld_line = 3) and no fills: one request, then every load merges.
Make fill_valid always 0: after two misses to different lines, ld_ready drops for a third.
